passages.t: ‘He remembers His covenant forever’: one story, told as God's faithfulness
passages.happening:
Psalms 105 and 106 are a pair. They tell the same story, from Egypt to the wilderness, twice. Psalm 105 tells it as the story of God's faithfulness. Psalm 106 tells it again as the story of Israel's failure. Read them together.

Psalm 105 has no heading. It opens with a burst of commands. “Give thanks to the LORD, call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations” (verse 1). Sing, tell, glory, seek (verses 2 to 4). “Remember the wonders He has done” (verse 5).

Then it names the one thing at the centre of the story. “He remembers His covenant forever, the word He ordained for a thousand generations” (verse 8), the covenant made with Abraham, sworn to Isaac and confirmed to Jacob (verses 9 to 10). The promise was a home: “I will give you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance” (verse 11).

When the family was small and homeless, wandering from one kingdom to another (verses 12 to 13), God guarded them. “He rebuked kings on their behalf” (verse 14), and said, ‘Do not touch My anointed ones’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The first fifteen verses appear again, with small changes, in 1 Chronicles 16, in the song sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem. The book page notes that the song in Chronicles is made of lines from Psalms 105, 96 and 106.

Many scholars think Psalm 105 was sung after the exile, when a people who had lost their land needed to hear that God's promise was ‘forever’. Others place it earlier, in the worship of the temple. The psalm itself names no year.

The ‘strangers in the land’ (verse 12) were Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who lived as outsiders among the towns of Canaan, owning no land, moving with their flocks. People like that had no one to protect them. Genesis tells how kings took notice of them, and how God stepped in (Genesis 12 and 20). In verse 15 God calls these wandering herdsmen ‘My anointed ones’ and ‘My prophets’. Titles for kings and prophets are given to a homeless family.

The land promised in verse 11 belongs to Israel's ancient story. The psalm speaks of God's faithfulness in that story. It does not speak to any modern border or state.
passages.later:
Hebrews says that Abraham “dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise” (Hebrews 11:9).

Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, praised God “to remember His holy covenant, the oath He swore to our father Abraham” (Luke 1:72-73). Paul writes, “if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:29).
passages.asks:
Psalm 105 tells the story by asking one question: what did God remember? He remembered his promise.

Look back at your own life the same way. Where were you small, and without protection, and God kept you anyway? Tell someone about it. That is what verse 1 asks: make known his deeds.

passages.t: Joseph, Egypt and the exodus: ‘For He remembered His holy promise’
passages.happening:
The psalm goes on through Genesis and Exodus. God sent famine (verse 16), but first “He sent a man before them” (verse 17): Joseph, sold as a slave. His feet were bruised in chains (verse 18) until God's word proved him right (verse 19). “The king sent and released him” (verse 20) and made him master of his house (verse 21).

Then Israel came to Egypt and grew strong (verses 23 to 24). The Egyptians turned against them (verse 25). God sent Moses and Aaron (verse 26), and the plagues: darkness, blood, frogs, gnats, hail, locusts, and last the death of the firstborn (verses 28 to 36).

“He brought Israel out with silver and gold” (verse 37). He led them with cloud and fire (verse 39), fed them with quail and bread from heaven (verse 40), and opened a rock for water (verse 41).

Why? “For He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant” (verse 42). “He brought forth His people with rejoicing” (verse 43). The psalm ends, “that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws. Hallelujah” (verse 45).
passages.hearers:
Notice what Psalm 105 leaves out. It does not mention the golden calf, the grumbling, or the forty years of wandering. That is not because the singer did not know. It is because this telling has one subject: what God did. Psalm 106 will tell the rest.

Egypt is called ‘the land of Ham’ (verses 23 and 27), because in Genesis, Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt, is listed among the sons of Ham (Genesis 10:6).

Joseph's story was a favourite. Sold by his brothers, he became the one who saved them. In Genesis he tells them, “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20). Psalm 105 tells his story in the same spirit.

The end of the psalm says why God did it all: so that his people would keep his ways. The rescue was not only from something. It was for something.
passages.later:
Stephen told the same story before the council in Jerusalem: the patriarchs “sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him and rescued him from all his troubles” (Acts 7:9-10).

Exodus says, “So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Exodus 2:24), the very word Psalm 105 keeps returning to.
passages.hard: Verse 25 says God turned the Egyptians' hearts to hate his people. Does God make people do evil? The psalm's point is that nothing, not even Egypt's cruelty, fell outside God's rule. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that God hardened it. Christians hold different views on how God's rule and human choice fit together. Scripture holds both: God is sovereign, and people are responsible for the evil they do.
passages.asks:
Joseph's feet were in chains before his story turned. If you are in a long, hard chapter, Psalm 105 does not promise you a quick end. It tells you that God's word ‘proved him right’ in the end, and that God remembers.

Read Psalm 106 next. Hold the two together: God's faithfulness, and our failures. Both are true, and the first is bigger.
